title: Double-slit fringe spacing
prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 8 established coherent light from two narrow slits, overlapping waves, and alternating bright and dark fringes.
Lesson 6 established that narrow gaps diffract waves and that spreading is stronger when wavelength is large compared with gap width.
Students already know wavelength and standard SI prefixes from Topics 1 and 7.
new_learning: Use the double-slit relationship λ = ax/D.
Convert slit separation, fringe spacing and wavelength into consistent units before substitution.
Rearrange the relationship and reason proportionally about fringe spacing.
not_yet_taught: recall and use d sin θ = nλ

blocks.title: One screen, two surprisingly different patterns
content: A red laser and a blue laser are used one at a time with the same two narrow slits and the same screen position. Which colour should give the wider bright-fringe spacing? A clear answer needs more than saying that both arrangements interfere.
Lesson 8 explains why the fringes exist. This lesson connects their measured spacing to wavelength, slit separation and screen distance.

figure.purpose: Create a visual prediction about how wavelength changes fringe spacing while holding the apparatus fixed.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison sketch of the same double-slit apparatus used with red and blue light. Show wider red fringe spacing and narrower blue fringe spacing qualitatively, with no numbers or formula.
figure.alt_text: The same double slits produce different fringe spacings for red and blue light.

blocks.title: Name the four quantities before calculating

definition.displayed_content: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase

content: This is the formula to remember for double-slit interference using light: λ = ax/D. Here λ is wavelength in metres, a is the separation of the two slits in metres, x is the separation of adjacent bright fringes or adjacent dark fringes in metres, and D is the perpendicular distance from the slits to the screen in metres.

The fringe spacing x is one interval, not the width of several intervals. The relationship uses the small-angle double-slit geometry represented by a screen much farther from the slits than the slit separation.

figure.purpose: Fix the spatial meaning of a, x and D before learners use the equation.
figure.brief: Rectangular annotated teacher sketch with laser, two slits separated by a, screen distance D measured perpendicularly, and x marked between two adjacent bright fringes. Use sparse coloured labels and do not include numerical values.
figure.alt_text: Double-slit geometry labels slit separation a, screen distance D and adjacent fringe spacing x.

blocks.title: A unit-safe wavelength calculation
content: Suppose a = 0.30 mm, x = 3.6 mm and D = 1.8 m. First convert both millimetre values: a = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m and x = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m.

Now substitute with units: λ = ax/D = (3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m)(3.6 × 10⁻³ m)/(1.8 m) = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. An independent magnitude check helps: 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻³ divided by a value near 1 gives about 10⁻⁷ m, a reasonable visible-light wavelength.
It is tempting to insert 0.30 and 3.6 directly because both values use millimetres. That fails because D is in metres and ax/D must finish in metres. Convert all lengths to one unit system first.

figure.purpose: Teach a repeatable unit-conversion and substitution layout.
figure.brief: Rectangular worked-layout sketch with four boxes: list data, convert mm to m, substitute into λ=ax/D with units, and check order of magnitude. Highlight powers of ten in colour.
figure.alt_text: A four-step layout converts lengths, calculates wavelength and checks its order of magnitude.

blocks.title: Measure several spaces, then find one
content: Fringes can be narrow, so measuring one gap is uncertain. Imagine the distance from the centre of bright fringe 1 to the centre of bright fringe 7 is 15.0 mm. Seven fringe centres contain six intervals, so x = 15.0 mm / 6 = 2.50 mm.

With a = 0.250 mm and D = 1.00 m, λ = (2.50 × 10⁻⁴ m)(2.50 × 10⁻³ m)/(1.00 m) = 6.25 × 10⁻⁷ m. Check the interval count by drawing seven marks and counting the six gaps between them. Counting fringes instead of gaps would make the wavelength too small.

figure.purpose: Make the distinction between fringe centres and fringe intervals visually unavoidable.
figure.brief: Rectangular strip with seven bright-fringe centre marks numbered 1 to 7, six coloured brackets between them, total distance 15.0 mm, and a side note x=15.0 mm/6. Do not show the final wavelength calculation.
figure.alt_text: Seven fringe centres span six equal fringe intervals.

blocks.title: The same relationship answers four kinds of question
content: Rearrange before substituting: x = λD/a, a = λD/x and D = ax/λ. Keep the physical meaning beside the symbols so that a and x are not swapped.

The form x = λD/a shows the trends. At fixed a, increasing λ or D increases x in direct proportion. At fixed λ and D, increasing a decreases x. For example, doubling D doubles x, but doubling a halves x.
A graph of x against D is a straight line through the origin in the ideal model, with gradient λ/a. A larger wavelength gives a steeper line when a is unchanged.

figure.purpose: Join algebraic rearrangement, proportional changes and graph gradient in one synthesis.
figure.brief: Rectangular three-panel teacher sketch: formula triangle-style rearrangements without hiding algebra, arrow table for λ, D and a changes, and two x-against-D straight lines labelled longer λ and shorter λ. Keep axes qualitative.
figure.alt_text: Rearrangements and graphs show how wavelength, screen distance and slit separation control fringe spacing.

blocks.title: A reliable route from pattern to physics
content: Use this route every time: identify what one fringe spacing means, count intervals if a longer span is measured, convert every length consistently, choose the needed rearrangement, substitute with units, then test the magnitude and proportional trend.

Diffraction at each narrow slit helps the two light waves spread and overlap. Interference produces the bright and dark pattern, and λ = ax/D describes its spacing. This equation does not describe diffraction-grating orders, and no grating equation is needed here.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the complete decision process and preserve the boundary between diffraction, interference and later grating work.
figure.brief: Rectangular flow diagram: count gaps, convert units, rearrange, substitute, check magnitude, check trend. Add a small side chain narrow slit spreads, waves overlap, fringes form. Explicitly label grating equation as later, without displaying it.
figure.alt_text: A calculation flow links measured fringe spacing to a checked double-slit result while reserving grating work for later.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

concepts_taught: unit-safe use and rearrangement of λ = ax/D
misconceptions_addressed: The number of visible fringe centres equals the number of fringe intervals.
Matching prefixes can be inserted without checking the unit of D.
Increasing slit separation increases fringe spacing.
The double-slit equation is a diffraction-grating equation.
skills_students_can_now_use: Convert nm, mm and m consistently.
Find one fringe spacing from a measured multi-fringe span.
Predict and explain proportional changes in x.
